added: #Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, 2 insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack.<ref>https://www.scienceprojects.org/simple-electric-circuit/</ref> The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, find one that is around 15-25 volts so a single battery can power them. <ref>https://www.scienceprojects.org/simple-electric-circuit/</ref>
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a 9-volt battery or battery pack. <ref>https://www.scienceprojects.org/simple-electric-circuit/</ref>
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire. <ref>https://www.scienceprojects.org/simple-electric-circuit/</ref>

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb.<ref>https://old.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/index.html</ref> The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a 9-volt battery or the battery pack. <ref>https://old.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/index.html</ref>

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.<ref>https://old.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/index.html</ref>

#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.<ref>https://old.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/index.html</ref>

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need 3 pieces of wire instead of 2 as well as a simple switch. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to install the switch.<ref>https://education.theiet.org/primary/teaching-resources/how-to-make-a-simple-electrical-circuit</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.<ref>https://education.theiet.org/primary/teaching-resources/how-to-make-a-simple-electrical-circuit</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.<ref>https://education.theiet.org/primary/teaching-resources/how-to-make-a-simple-electrical-circuit</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.<ref>https://education.theiet.org/primary/teaching-resources/how-to-make-a-simple-electrical-circuit</ref>

== Steps ==
=== Building a Simple Circuit with a Battery ===

#Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, 2 insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, find one that is around 15-25 volts so a single battery can power them.
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a 9-volt battery or battery pack.

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about {{convert|1|in|cm}} of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#* If you don’t have wire strippers, you can carefully use scissors to cut off the insulation.
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire.

#Install batteries into the battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a 9-volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Installing a Switch ===

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need 3 pieces of wire instead of 2 as well as a simple switch. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to install the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Troubleshooting Your Circuit ===

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12 Version 2.jpg|center]]

=== Building a Simple Circuit with a Battery ===

#Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, 2 insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, find one that is around 15-25 volts so a single battery can power them.
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a 9-volt battery or battery pack.

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about {{convert|1|in|cm}} of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* If you don’t have wire strippers, you can carefully use scissors to cut off the insulation.
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire.

#Install batteries into the battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a 9-volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Installing a Switch ===

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need 3 pieces of wire instead of 2 as well as a simple switch. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to install the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref> Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Troubleshooting Your Circuit ===

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12.jpg|center]]
#* Make sure screws are tightened down to maintain contact.
#* In some cases, you may need to strip more of the insulation off the wire.

#Check the filament in your light bulb. Your bulb will not light if the filament is broken. Hold the bulb up to the light and ensure the filament is one connected piece. Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Test the charge of the battery. If the battery is dead or low on charge, it might not have enough power to light the bulb. Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a 9-volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Installing a Switch ===

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need 3 pieces of wire instead of 2 as well as a simple switch. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to install the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref> Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Troubleshooting Your Circuit ===

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12.jpg|center]]
#* Make sure screws are tightened down to maintain contact.
#* In some cases, you may need to strip more of the insulation off the wire.

#Check the filament in your light bulb. Your bulb will not light if the filament is broken. Hold the bulb up to the light and ensure the filament is one connected piece. Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Test the charge of the battery. If the battery is dead or low on charge, it might not have enough power to light the bulb. Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]

=== Building a Simple Circuit with a Battery ===

#Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, two insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, keep in mind the amount of power your battery emits.
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a nine volt battery or battery pack.

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about an inch of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* If you don’t have wire strippers, you can carefully use scissors to cut off the insulation.
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire.

#Install batteries into battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a nine volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remain in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]

#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.

#* In some cases, you may need to strip more of the insulation off the wire.

Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]

== Steps ==
=== Building a Simple Circuit with a Battery ===

#Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, two insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, keep in mind the amount of power your battery emits.
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a nine volt battery or battery pack.

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about an inch of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* If you don’t have wire strippers, you can carefully use scissors to cut off the insulation.
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire.

#Install batteries into battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a nine volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remain in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Installing a Switch ===

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need three pieces of wire instead of two. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to installing the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref> Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Troubleshooting Your Circuit ===

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12.jpg|center]]
#* Make sure screws are tightened down to maintain contact.
#* In some cases, you may need to strip more of the insulation off the wire.

#Check the filament in your light bulb. Your bulb will not light if the filament is broken. Hold the bulb up to the light and ensure the filament is one connected piece. Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Test the charge of the battery. If the battery is dead or low on charge, it might not have enough power to light the bulb. Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]

*Don't touch the light bulb when lit as it will be hot.

=== Building a Simple Circuit with a Battery ===

#Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, two insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* When choosing a light bulb, keep in mind the amount of power your battery emits.
#* To simplify the wire attachment process, use a battery snap with wires pre-attached and a nine volt battery or battery pack.

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about an inch of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* If you don’t have wire strippers, you can carefully use scissors to cut off the insulation.
#* Be careful not to cut all the way through the wire.

#Install batteries into battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#* Alternatively, if you are using a battery snap, snap the end onto the end of a nine volt battery or the battery pack.

#* Use caution while building your circuit. Although unlikely, it is possible to get a very small shock if you touch the wire directly while attached to the battery. You can avoid this by only touching the insulated part of the wire or removing the batteries until you install the light bulb.

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remain in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Installing a Switch ===

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need three pieces of wire instead of two. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to installing the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref> Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]
#* Light bulbs can heat up quickly so be careful when installing and removing the bulb.
#* If the bulb doesn’t light, check to make sure the wires are touching the ends of the battery and in contact with the metal of the screws.
=== Troubleshooting Your Circuit ===

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12.jpg|center]]
#* Make sure screws are tightened down to maintain contact.
#* In some cases, you may need to strip more of the insulation off the wire.

#Check the filament in your light bulb. Your bulb will not light if the filament is broken. Hold the bulb up to the light and ensure the filament is one connected piece. Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Test the charge of the battery. If the battery is dead or low on charge, it might not have enough power to light the bulb. Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]

added: #Gather the necessary materials. To build a simple circuit, you will need a power source, two insulated wires, a light bulb, and a light bulb holder. A power source can be any type of battery or battery pack. The rest of the materials can be found at your local hardware store.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the insulated wires. In order for your circuit to work properly, the wires need to be totally exposed so you must strip the ends. Using wire strippers, remove about an inch of the insulation from the ends of each wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Install batteries into battery pack. Depending on the type of batteries you are using, you may be able to skip this step. If you are using multiple batteries, you will need a power pack to hold the batteries. Push each battery in by the side taking care to put the positive and negative ends in the correct orientation.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach your wires to the battery pack. The wires will be conducting your electric current from the batteries to the light bulb. The easiest way to attach the wires is to use electrical tape. Attach the end of one wire to one side of the battery, making sure that the wire maintains contact with the metal of the battery. Repeat with the other wire on the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Fasten the other end of the wire to the metal screw of the bulb holder. Take the exposed metal end of each wire and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref>  Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the metal of the wires remain in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 6.jpg|center]]

#Gather the materials. To install the switch, you will need three pieces of wire instead of two. Once you strip the wires and get them attached to the battery pack you can proceed to installing the switch.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Install the switch. Take the exposed metal end of one of the wires from the battery pack and bend it into a U-shape.<ref>http://www.miniscience.com/kits/KITSEC/</ref> Loosen the screw on the switch and slip the U-shape of the wire underneath. Tighten the screw making sure that the metal of the wire remains in contact with the screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Attach the extra third wire to the switch. Bend each of the metal ends of the wire into a U-shape. Slip the U-shape under the second screw of the switch to attach it. Tighten the screw ensuring the metal of the screw stays in contact with the metal of the wire.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Hook up the light bulb. Take the end of each wire (one from the battery and one from the switch) and bend it into a U-shape. Loosen each screw on the light bulb holder just enough to slip the U-shape of the wire around the screw. Each wire will be attached to its own screw. Tighten the screw, ensuring that the wires remain in contact with the metal screw.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Test your circuit. Screw the light bulb into its holder until it is tight. Flip the switch! If your circuit is hooked up properly, the bulb should light up when fully screwed into its socket.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 11.jpg|center]]

#Make sure all of the wires are connected properly. In order to complete the circuit, all wires must be touching the metal parts of each component. If your bulb doesn’t light up, check each side of the battery and the screws on the bulb holder to make sure the wires are in contact with metal.<ref>https://www.sparkfun.com/tutorials/226</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 12.jpg|center]]

#Check the filament in your light bulb. Your bulb will not light if the filament is broken. Hold the bulb up to the light and ensure the filament is one connected piece. Try replacing the bulb with a new one. If the bulb isn’t the problem, proceed to the next troubleshooting step.[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Test the charge of the battery. If the battery is dead or low on charge, it might not have enough power to light the bulb. Using a battery tester, check the charge or just replace the battery with a new one. If this was the problem, your bulb should light immediately after replacing the battery.<ref> http://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/reference/chpt-8/likely-failures-in-proven-systems/</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electrical Circuit Step 14.jpg|center]]
